title: Perspectives: Liberal, Socialist, Marxist, Radical Humanist, Dalit

cards.h: Five readings of the same struggle
cards.b:
Every group in the national movement asked: Freedom from whom, for whom, and to do what? The British were the obvious enemy, but liberals, socialists, Marxists, radical humanists and Dalit leaders also named other enemies: poverty, capital, caste, superstition.

This lesson covers five perspectives. For each, learn the leaders, their key text or organisation, what they thought nationalism was for, and where they differed from Gandhi and the Congress.

Examiners like comparative questions, such as "Compare Gandhi and Ambedkar on the caste question" or "Evaluate the Marxist critique of the Indian National Congress". A matrix of perspective by theme will help you answer quickly.

The differences can be reduced to three questions: What is the main contradiction (colonial rule, class, caste, or the loss of individual freedom)? Who is the agent of change (the educated elite, workers and peasants, the rational individual, the oppressed castes)? What is the method (constitutional reform, mass action, revolution, education and law)?

The early Congress was liberal. Dadabhai Naoroji, Mahadev Govind Ranade, G.K. Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta and Surendranath Banerjea believed in British ideals of law, representation and free speech, and asked Britain to live up to them.

  • Economic nationalism: Naoroji's drain theory, R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India (1902-04).
  • Social reform: Ranade and Gokhale (Servants of India Society, 1905) stressed that political freedom needs social reform.
  • Method: gradual, constitutional, with an emphasis on rights and councils.
  • Later liberals: after 1918 many left the Congress, forming the National Liberal Federation (1919). Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar were prominent.

Critique: too elitist, dependent on British goodwill, and slow. Yet the liberals' constitutionalism, rule of law and individual rights fed straight into the Constitution of 1950.

Socialist ideas grew among Congress members in the 1920s and 1930s, driven by the Russian Revolution, the Depression and Nehru's influence (his 1927 visit to the USSR; presidency of Lucknow 1936).

The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) was founded in 1934 inside the Congress, with Acharya Narendra Dev, Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Achyut Patwardhan, Asoka Mehta and others. Its aims:

  • Make the Congress a mass organisation of workers and peasants.
  • Link freedom with the removal of economic exploitation: abolition of zamindari, nationalisation of key industries.
  • Use Marxian analysis but reject its dictatorship. They kept faith in democracy and in Gandhi's mass action, but not his trusteeship.

Jayaprakash Narayan's Why Socialism? (1936) was a key text. The socialists played a big part in the Quit India underground (1942).

cards.h: Lohia and JP: Indian socialism's own path
cards.b:
Ram Manohar Lohia (1910-67)

In Wheel of History (1955) he argued that caste and class are linked in India and that ownership alone does not explain power. He wanted a socialism of the "four pillars" (chaukhamba state): village, district, province and centre. He stressed small-unit technology, seven revolutions (against inequality of caste, class, sex, colour, colonialism, arms and for civil liberty), and special opportunities (vishesh avsar) for backward castes, women and minorities. Hence the slogan of 60 per cent reserved for the backward.

Jayaprakash Narayan (1902-79)

After Marxism he turned to Gandhian ideas: Sarvodaya in the early 1950s (he pledged his life, jeevandan, to Vinoba's movement in 1954), and partyless democracy in A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959). In 1974-75 he called for Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti).

• Origins: M.N. Roy helped form a Communist group at Tashkent (1920). The CPI was formally founded in India in Kanpur in 1925. Leaders: S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, S.V. Ghate, P.C. Joshi. The party was banned in the 1930s and faced the Kanpur and Meerut cases.
  • Analysis: Marxist writers saw British rule as colonial exploitation and the Indian capitalists as a class with divided interests. R.P. Dutt's India Today (1940) argued the bourgeoisie compromised with imperialism. A.R. Desai's Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948) read nationalism through class. D.D. Kosambi studied history from below.
  • Critique of Congress: a bourgeois party, using the masses for its own aims and stopping movements before they went too far (Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Chauri Chaura).
  • Strategy: unite workers and peasants, but the CPI's line shifted: the "Peoples' War" line of 1942 (supporting the war effort after the USSR was attacked) isolated it from Quit India.

• Strengths: it highlighted exploitation, class and the role of workers and peasants. Marxists pushed the freedom movement to take up land reform and labour rights. Poverty and economic issues became part of the nationalist programme.
  • Weaknesses: it underplayed caste, religion and culture. It applied European class categories mechanically. Gramsci-influenced later Marxists admit that Congress built a hegemonic bloc with real mass support, not mere manipulation.
  • The Comintern problem: the line from Moscow (e.g., 1928 "sectarian" turn, Calcutta Thesis 1948) often fitted India poorly.
  • Dalit critique: Ambedkar called Marxism blind to caste (see his "Buddha or Karl Marx", 1956). He saw capitalism and Brahminism as twin enemies of the labouring poor.

The fair verdict: Marxism enriched the debate and economic analysis, but fit India only partly.

cards.h: The radical humanist perspective: M.N. Roy
cards.b:
Manabendra Nath Roy (1887-1954) began as a Bengal revolutionary, became a founder of the Mexican and the Indian communist parties, and a Comintern leader. He clashed with Lenin at the Second Comintern Congress (1920), over whether colonial nationalists could be allies. Expelled from the Comintern in 1929, he returned to India in 1930, was jailed (1931-36), joined Congress, then left. He formed the Radical Democratic Party (1940).

His change in thought: from Marxism to Radical Humanism or New Humanism (1946-47; the 22 Theses). Core ideas:

  • Man is the measure of all things, and is rational and moral.
  • Freedom of the individual is the goal of social progress, not class or party.
  • Rejection of party politics: replace it with people's committees (Politics, Power and Parties, 1960) and a cooperative economy.
  • Basis: science, reason, and ethics, not religion.

Detailed in lesson 0-8-5.

cards.h: The Dalit perspective: Phule to Ambedkar
cards.b:
• Jotirao Phule (1827-90): Gulamgiri (1873) described caste as Brahmin enslavement of the shudras and atishudras. Founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873). With Savitribai Phule he began girls' schooling in 1848.
  • South India: Sri Narayana Guru ("one caste, one religion, one god"; his 1888 consecration of a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram challenged Brahmin monopoly), Ayyankali, Periyar E.V. Ramasamy's Self-Respect Movement (1925) and Iyothee Thass.
  • B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956): Mooknayak (1920), Mahad satyagraha (1927, for water, with a burning of the Manusmriti), Kalaram temple entry at Nashik (1930), Poona Pact (1932), Independent Labour Party (1936), Annihilation of Caste (1936), and the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). He gave his views in What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945).

Core claim: political freedom without social freedom is hollow. The depressed classes needed their own political safeguards. Ambedkar embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956 at Nagpur.

cards.h: Gandhi and Ambedkar on caste and nationalism
cards.b:
• Diagnosis: Gandhi first defended the varna order but sought to remove untouchability (he called Dalits Harijans). Ambedkar called for annihilation of caste itself.
  • Remedy: Gandhi trusted a change of heart among caste Hindus and the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932). Ambedkar demanded legal safeguards, separate electorates and political power.
  • Poona Pact (1932): after Gandhi's fast, Ambedkar gave up separate electorates in return for reserved seats (148 in provincial legislatures, up from 71).
  • Village: Gandhi romanticised it; Ambedkar saw it as a centre of oppression.

Link back to the others: socialists such as Lohia took caste more seriously after independence. Marxists, for their part, were criticised for not seeing it earlier.

• Liberal: constitutionalism, free press and the rule of law, defended in cases like Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Puttaswamy (2017).
  • Socialist: the Janata and Janata Dal family, Lohia's social justice politics and Mandal (1990), and welfare rights. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "socialist" to the Preamble.
  • Marxist: the Left parties (CPI, CPI(M)) and trade unions, with Kerala as their historic stronghold. Maoist groups claim the Naxalbari legacy.
  • Radical Humanist: ideas on decentralisation and civil liberties groups.
  • Dalit: Ambedkar's Constitution is central. Dalit political assertion includes the Bahujan Samaj Party (1984) and the 2018 debate on the SC/ST Atrocities Act. Reservation continues (see lesson 0-3-1).

The caste enumeration decision in the next Census (announced April 2025) revived these debates.

"Dalit perspectives on nationalism differ sharply from the mainstream." Discuss.
Examine the Marxist critique of the Indian national movement.
Evaluate M.N. Roy's contribution as a radical humanist.
Compare Gandhi's and Ambedkar's approaches to the caste question.

Structure: open with the framing questions (enemy, agent, method). For each perspective give leaders, key text, central claim and critique, in a table if possible. Always link to Gandhi and the Congress for comparison. Keep one balanced paragraph: how each perspective widened the aims of the movement, and how the Constitution drew on all of them.

quiz.q: The Congress Socialist Party was founded in…
quiz.w: Inside the Congress, by JP, Narendra Dev, Lohia and others.

quiz.q: Which book by R.P. Dutt gave a Marxist analysis of British rule in India?
quiz.w: It argued that the bourgeoisie compromised with imperialism.

quiz.q: Lohia's Wheel of History was published in…
Partyless democracy and Sarvodaya are linked with…
quiz.w: JP's A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959).

quiz.q: The Radical Democratic Party (1940) was founded by…
M.N. Roy disagreed with Lenin at the Second Comintern Congress on…
quiz.w: Roy doubted that bourgeois nationalists were reliable allies.
Jotirao Phule, founder of the Satyashodhak Samaj.

o: Access to a public water tank

quiz.q: Under the Poona Pact, Ambedkar agreed to…
o: Give up separate electorates for reserved seats

quiz.q: Annihilation of Caste was written in…
quiz.w: It was a speech for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal that was never delivered.
